extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of a 19th-century popular magazine interested in literature and popular medicine
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical examples for writing and reading magazine-length essays on literature and popular science; includes norms of literary criticism (honesty, independence of taste) and some medical-observational criteria about obesity's effects. Useful for essayists, critics, and informed lay readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sham admiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pretend admiration where you do not feel it; abstain from expressing an opinion that is not your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author repeatedly urges honesty: better to be honest though it may expose one to ridicule than to lie; example of a young lady confessing she never really laughed at 'John Gilpin' or Goldsmith's 'Elegy on a Mad Dog' despite pretending to do so. Pithy dicta: 'everybody has a right to his own opinion' and one can 'abstain from expressing an opinion that is not his own.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer independent judgment over mere adhesion to received opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid mechanical adherence to authority or received verdicts; form opinions from direct engagement rather than rote repetition of past acclaim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The habit of adhesion to received opinion 'strikes at the root of independence of thought' and makes public taste mechanical. Examples: works 'more praised than read' (Walter Scott, others); critics and readers should not repeat the 'cuckoo cry' of fashionable comparisons without personal verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate praise to avoid creating disappointed readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Extravagant, vehem ent, or dogmatic praise of works does harm by raising impossible expectations and driving readers away when they fail to find unrivaled beauties in every sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overblown laudation leads students/readers to attempt works, fail to find the expected beauties, and stop reading (they conclude 'I have been deceived' or 'I must be a born fool'). The author warns critics that vehemence and exaggeration drive the weak into falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read primary works before endorsing or comparing them
rubrics_metrics.description: Before endorsing, canonizing, or comparing works to older masterpieces, one should actually read them; don't rely on secondhand reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes many 'great' books are subscribed to more often than believed and often not actually read. Examples include the public echoing Bias and Company about Godwin's 'Caleb Williams' and other fashionable comparisons without firsthand reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected jargon and artificial art-talk in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not discourse about literature in an affected, pinchbeck, or fashionably-technical style; plain, honest speech is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author condemns the 'pinchbeck and affected style' of art-talk that infects literary discussion, likening it to retail jargon (an anecdote about a sideboard 'having a Chippendale feeling in it'). Such jargon creates distance from genuine taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have the courage to dissent from canonical opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable and even commendable to dissent from classical or canonical judgments when one genuinely does not admire a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites examples where great authorities (Dr. Johnson, Macaulay) admitted lack of admiration for widely esteemed works, arguing humbler folk should have courage to hold honest views rather than lie. Encourages free expression of opinion rather than mouthing conventional praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include physical constitution when analyzing fictional character behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: When interpreting a character's motives or actions, critics should consider the character's physical organization or constitution as a potentially decisive explanatory factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied centrally to Hamlet: Shakespeare 'never failed to make the physique conform to the character.' The essay argues that neglecting corporeal factors (e.g., corpulence) has led commentators astray; the body can explain apparent contradictions between thought and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret Hamlet's procrastination in light of his physicality ('too solid flesh')
rubrics_metrics.description: Read Hamlet's 'fat' and 'scant of breath' as key explanatory elements: his obesity/lymphatic temperament produces inertia that limits action despite high intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author proposes that Hamlet's chronic inaction is accounted for by being 'weight ed down with a non-executive or lymphatic temperament' — 'the inertia of fat' metaphorically and physiologically explains the mismatch between Hamlet's clear reasoning and failure to act. Textual cues cited: 'too too solid flesh,' Ophelia's 'bulk' line, the queen offering a 'napkin' to wipe perspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray/stage characters faithful to the textual physical description
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists and actors should represent characters in accordance with the text's physical descriptions rather than imposing fashionable, ill-supported types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticizes painters and actors for depicting Hamlet as 'fleshless and dark-hued' or bilious and nervous; argues a true Shakespearean Hamlet would be 'grunting and sweating under his weary load of life.' Example: Fechter's rare attempt to recall Hamlet's nationality via a flaxen wig.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize adipose deposits can impair sensory functions (anosmia, deafness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical observers should consider excessive fatty deposits as a cause of impaired smell and hearing through infiltration of olfactory cells and mechanical obstruction of air passages/Eustachian tubes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References Dr. W. Ogle's five cases of anosmia from fatty deposits permeating olfactory apparatus cells; Dr. Harvey's cases of deafness due to nasal obstruction from adipose deposit interfering with air entrance to Eustachian tubes. Explains sympathetic mucous membrane connections transmitting local pathology to distant sensory effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand obesity's adverse effects on circulation and general vitality
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess adipose tissue overtaxes the capillary network and circulation, producing comparative weakness: shortness of breath, palpitation, anemia, reduced reparative capacity, and predisposition to fatty degeneration of heart/muscle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative numeric example (man 5'10" normal 169 lb vs 300 lb obese) shows capillaries required for superfluous fat must draw blood from vessels sized for original mass, leading to enfeebled circulation. The author links these effects to impaired activity and reduced resistance to injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate 'good' fat from 'bad' fat in assessing health implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all bodily fat is equal: 'good fat' (e.g., that of a florid person) is less harmful, whereas flabby, anemic-associated fat ('bad fat') indicates poorer health, as seen in chronic alcoholics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author advises clinicians/readers to distinguish types of fat by appearance and associated physiology; 'bad fat' often accompanies unwholesome looks and disease states, while some adiposity may be benign within limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use microscopic examination to identify fatty degeneration
rubrics_metrics.description: Microscopy is essential for scientifically understanding and diagnosing fatty degeneration (especially of the heart and muscular tissues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: only with careful application of the microscope were investigators able to understand the disease now called 'fatty degeneration.' This is offered as methodological guidance to medical observers investigating adipose-related pathology.
